Circle Of Similitude 1

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: two circles and a third circle between them show four surprising equalities.
How to play: Drag the five dots with a mouse or finger, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Press the statement buttons to show each idea, and Check all to see the equal numbers.
Look for the math

Take any point T on the orange circle between the two grey ones. Four things that look unrelated turn out to be equal: two angles, two distances from a line, and two lengths on a chord. Drag the dots and the equalities never break.

Where the middle circle comes from

The two common tangents that cross between the circles meet at the internal centre P; the two that do not cross meet at the external centre Q. Both are homothety centres: from P or Q one circle looks like a scaled copy of the other. The orange circle has PQ as its diameter, so its centre is the midpoint of P and Q and its radius is |PQ| / 2. It is also the Apollonian circle of the two centres for the ratio r1 / r2: every T on it satisfies TO1 / TO2 = r1 / r2. The logic test checks this at hundreds of positions, including tilted circles that the old applet could not draw.

Right angles where the circles cross

The grey circle drawn on O1O2 as a diameter meets the orange circle at E and F. Statement 1 says the two circles are orthogonal: the lines from E (or F) to the two centres make a right angle. In numbers, dist(CS, CM)² = R² + RM², where CM is the midpoint of O1O2. The test finds the difference smaller than a millionth at every configuration it tries, so the page's claim holds.

The angle cut in half

From T draw the two tangents to each circle. They touch the first circle at L1 and M1, and the second at L2 and M2. Pairing L1 with L2 and M1 with M2, statement 2 says the line TP cuts both angles at T in half: angle L1 T P = angle P T L2. The old applet showed only one pair at a time; the L/M button here switches between them, and Check all speaks the two matching angles. The reason is that on the Apollonian circle TP is an angle bisector of O1 T O2, while TO1 and TO2 bisect the two tangent angles.

Equal lengths, equal distances

The radical axis is the line where the two circles have the same power. Statement 3 says L1 and L2 are the same distance from it, so the midpoint of L1L2 lies on it. Statement 4 says the line L1L2 cuts the circles again at K1 and K2 with L1K1 = L2K2; statement 4' says the same thing as t(L1, c2) = t(L2, c1), where t is the length of a tangent segment. Each equality holds for both pairs in the logic test, and so does the page's converse: the tangents at L1 and L2 meet back on the orange circle.

Three small differences from the old applet are worth saying. Its page calls these "three" properties but shows four statements and four checkboxes; this port keeps all four. It starts with two equal circles, which sends Q to infinity and hides the construction although the page asks for different radii, so this port starts with unequal radii. Its radical-axis line is always vertical, even when the centres are tilted; this port draws the true line perpendicular to O1O2. Its four centre and radius dots can only slide horizontally; ours keep that same behaviour.

Press Statement 4, then drag T right round the orange circle: watch the two green chord parts stay the same length while their position changes.
